proposed_edges.relationship: In Trial by Fire and Water (1986) Bartlett labels Peter Brown's account of the ordeal as a consensus-building device that lapsed as coercive authority grew ‘the functionalist approach’ and rejects it, tying the ordeal's spread instead to the growth of royal power (as read by Heikki Pihlajamäki, 1997).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mediated through a named scholarly reader; Bartlett's book is unread. Heikki Pihlajamäki, Evidence, Crime, and the Legal Profession (Lund: Institutet för rättshistorisk forskning, Rättshistoriskt bibliotek 54, 1997), p. 33, read in the Olin Foundation's own digital edition: ‘Peter Brown departs from the idea that the medieval world at the time of ordeals was consensus-minded’, ordeals maintaining group cohesion until coercive authority made them unnecessary (n. 30: Brown 1982, p. 324, i.e. ‘Society and the Supernatural’, reprinted in Society and the Holy in Late Antiquity); ‘Bartlett calls this “the functionalist approach” and rejects it’, linking the increased use of ordeals to royal power and calling the ordeal an ‘adjunct of royal power’ (n. 31: Bartlett 1988, pp. 34–43, the paperback of the 1986 Clarendon book; n. 32: Bartlett 1988, pp. 70–102). Pihlajamäki's footnote numbering is partly garbled in the digital text, so the exact Bartlett page ranges are his and uncollated. Brown's essay (cited by Pihlajamäki as Brown 1982) and Bartlett's chapters remain unread; the claim is Pihlajamäki's account of Bartlett's argument, not a fresh reading of either original. Pihlajamäki also notes difficulties in Bartlett's own explanation of abolition; not used here.

review.reason: Pihlajamäki p. 33 re-fetched in the Institutet för rättshistorisk forskning/Olin Foundation's own digital edition (publisher route; acceptable). Verbatim: 'Peter Brown departs from the idea that the medieval world at the time of ordeals was consensus-minded'; 'Bartlett calls this “the functionalist approach” and rejects it by showing that in fact the increased use of ordeals is seen to be in close connection with the growth of royal power'; 'adjunct of royal power'; notes 30 (Brown 1982 p. 324), 31 (Bartlett 1988 pp. 34–43), 32 (Bartlett 1988 pp. 70–102). The Peter Brown in the source is the late-antique historian (Brown 1982 = Society and the Holy), matching the endpoint. The relationship is attributed ('as read by Heikki Pihlajamäki, 1997') and the reader is substantive (a legal historian's monograph discussing Bartlett's argument at length). Single second-hand reader, attributed: acceptable under the review rule. Palmer's 1989 Michigan Law Review review would corroborate if it becomes readable.
